To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
citizen science has the potential to be a useful ecological research tool, but that the benefits of citizen science are not without costs.

(a) large-scale, volunteer-based ecological research has the potential to provide a unique perspective to the field of ecology; (b) large-scale, citizen science has been used to address questions about the impacts of global change, but is also applicable to other questions; (c) citizen science data sets are subject to error and bias; and (d) citizen science data can be used to answer questions that would otherwise be impossible to study.

(1) citizen science has the potential to produce large-scale, longitudinal data sets that are useful for understanding the impacts of current global "experiments," such as habitat loss and climate change, and (2) these data sets are best used to answer questions about distribution, abundance, and change, and are most useful in conjunction with more localized, hypothesis-driven research.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the role of citizen science in ecological field research, and how citizen science data can be used to answer questions about the distribution, abundance, and behavior of organisms across space and time.

the development and application of statistical methods for the analysis of data from large scale ecological studies, with particular emphasis on the analysis of ecological data collected in a citizen science framework.
the role of citizen science in the field of ecology.

citizen science has great potential to address ecological questions at scales not possible by other means, and it is an important component of a comprehensive approach to ecological research.
